work.author: Severian of Gabala
work.title: In Temptationem Domini Nostri Iesu Christi

paragraphs.text: Our Lord and Saviour Jesus Christ went out into the desert, arming himself against the devil. For his is the voice that says: "No one can plunder the goods of the strong man unless he first boldly binds the strong man, and then he will plunder his goods." So he brings in the humanity, the human creature that he had put on. He brings it into the desert, making it a citizen of the victory over the devil [?], making the body a weapon against the demons. Now pay close attention. While he was contending, he nowhere showed the face of his divine rank. If you want to see that the devil was dealing not with the only-begotten Son of God but with the man, listen with all your ears to what the devil says: "If you are the Son of God, command these stones to become bread." But the Saviour hid his rank and put forward the plan of his incarnation, for everywhere his aim was this: to show himself contending, and to see this fallen one crowned. He says to him: "Man shall not live by bread alone, but by every word that comes from the mouth of God." He contends as in the person of humanity. If he had been speaking about his rank, he would have said, "The Son of God shall not live by bread alone." But because he wanted to show that man too wins the crown, and so to show him contending and to bestow on him the prizes of victory, he says: "Man shall not live by bread alone." "I too am a man," he is saying, "and I have no need of bread. The word of God is enough to nourish me."

See how the evil one works. The devil argues from reasoning, but Christ from the Scriptures. This marks the difference between the Church and the heretics: the heretics are dialecticians; the Church believes.

He said to the Son of God, "Let these stones become bread." The argument followed logically, for it is fitting for the Son of God even to transform things. But the Saviour, preferring truth to reasoning, turns to the testimony of the Scriptures and says to him: "Man shall not live by bread alone, but by every word that comes from the mouth of God."

After this, when the devil had been refuted, he too turns to the Scriptures. Having led him up to the pinnacle of the temple, he says to him: "If you are the Son of God, throw yourself down from here." And after this, "you will not be hurt," he says, "for this is written." See how the devil uses another's weapons, and keep this in mind. "It is written that he will command his angels concerning you, and on their hands they will bear you up, lest you strike your foot against a stone."

Say the next part too, devil. Do you not know how the passage continues? Why do you hide it, like the heretic who brings forward only what agrees with his own way of thinking? He hides the continuation, because it declares his overthrow. "It is written that he will command his angels concerning you, and on their hands they will bear you up, lest you strike your foot against a stone." Read what follows as well: "You will tread on the asp and the basilisk, and you will trample the lion and the dragon." But since the prophecy is against the devil, he does not bring forward what is against him, only what he thought was in his favour.

The Saviour says to him: "It is written: You shall not put the Lord your God to the test." Many think he was telling the devil himself, "Do not tempt the Lord your God," and they want to apply the saying to the rank of the Only-begotten. But we do not take it as referring to his rank. We do not deny his rank; rather, we confess his power. It is not from this saying that the Only-begotten is shown to be Lord and God, for there are countless testimonies proclaiming his rank. Here, though, he speaks in the person of humanity, since the other had said, "Throw yourself down from here. Let us see, then, whether you come to harm [?]. It is written that he will command his angels concerning you." In the person of humanity he says, "You shall not put the Lord your God to the test," as if to say: "It is written that I, a man, must not tempt God. I will not throw myself down, so that I may not tempt God. I do not tempt him; I do not put him to the proof. Even if I were able to help myself, this would be foreign to piety." He says this not from his divine rank but from his human appearance.
"I am a man and I am righteous, and I do not tempt God." For the righteous have never tempted God. They bear necessity when it comes upon them, and if God wishes to test them, they accept it.

Did those who were rescued from the fiery furnace, or from some other trial, throw themselves in to put God to the test? Did Daniel say, "Throw me into the lions' den"? Or did the three youths say, "Throw us into the fiery furnace, for God will rescue us"? If they had handed themselves over, it would have been presumption that armed them, not piety that equipped them. Nebuchadnezzar answered the three martyrs, saying: "Whenever you hear the sound of the trumpet, pipe and lyre, harp and psaltery, bagpipe and every kind of music, fall down and worship the image." When he had said this, he added: "And who is the god who will deliver you out of my hands?" The martyrs answer: "Be it known to you, O king, that we do not serve your gods and we do not worship the image that you have set up. For there is a God who will be able to deliver us." They did not say, "who will deliver us," but "who is able."

Do you see a pious mind? "He is able to deliver us," they say, "and if he does not wish to, we will not on that account deny our piety. For we bear witness to our resolve before the One who is able, but we do not put him to the test. We bear witness to his power."

"I know that he is able, but I do not force his will. There is a God who is able to deliver us, and even if not, be it known to you, O king, that we do not serve your gods, and we do not worship the golden image that you have set up." So the righteous did not tempt God. They accepted the calamity that came upon them, and beyond all expectation they enjoyed his kindness.

So the Saviour says in the person of humanity, "You shall not tempt the Lord your God." By adding "It is written: You shall not put the Lord your God to the test," he showed that the saying was not addressed to the demon, and that the title refers to the plan of the incarnation [?].

So the one who was tempting God received a second arrow after the first, and went away. Or rather, he did not go away, but stayed on in his shamelessness, for it is characteristic of wickedness to press on with its own madness. He takes the Lord again to a very high mountain and shows him all the kingdoms of the world and their glory in a moment of time.

How did he show them? For God all things are possible, but how was it easy for the devil to show them? The text does not say, "Jesus saw." He who encompasses all things could have seen all things while standing in one place, in a single corner. But I am asking how the devil showed him the kingdoms. Even if someone climbs to a high place and looks at all the cities, he sees the cattle grazing between them [?]. How, then, did the devil show such a vast and varied display in a moment of time? It is easy for the devil to change his form for the purposes of wickedness. If he disguises himself as an angel of light, much more can he take the form of a visible illusion.

Then he says: "All these I will give you, if you fall down and worship me." Because he was speaking to humanity, he puts forward this third temptation too, and says: "All these I will give you, if you fall down and worship me." Bitter as the devil's words are, they are a safeguard, not for him who speaks them but for us who hear them: "if you fall down and worship me."

So, then, there is no way to worship him without first falling? "All these I will give you, if you fall down and worship me." He promises a fall first, and then a gift. But the Saviour, putting an end to the full measure of his madness, says to him, "Go away, Satan." And this "Go away, Satan" rings out as God's own sentence. "For it is written: You shall worship the Lord your God and serve him alone." And the devil departed from him.

He drives him off with a word, just as later he threw back with a word the devil's sons, the Jews who fought against God. When they said, "Where is Jesus?" he said to them, "I am he," and that word threw them all backward. So too with the devil: "Go away, Satan," and the word drove him out and hurled him backward, and the devil departed from him until an opportune time.

This was written for our safety. Everywhere, through the image that he took on, he leaves us a pattern of life and teaches you. When you have wrestled with the devil and won, you must not grow careless, but must know that he lifts his head again after the victory. Often, indeed, when a strong craving or desire or some other passion assails us and grapples with us as in a wrestling match, the mind brings vigorous reason to bear and overcomes the passions, and then the very one who has just won is defeated by another assault. Therefore we must not grow careless, but must know that the victory lasts only for a time, and the security only for a time. Victory over the passions is temporary. As long as we are in the world, we both win and keep wrestling. Perfect victory comes at the end of the contests. That is why Paul, even while winning, was not careless, but was anxious about the future and said: "So I run, not aimlessly; so I box, not as one beating the air; but I discipline my body and bring it into subjection, lest after preaching to others I myself should be disqualified." But when he had run to the end of the contests and was about to be crowned, he said: "I have fought the good fight, I have finished the race, I have kept the faith."

So, brothers, the completion of the contests is the completion of life. Do not think that anyone is crowned before his death, since Scripture says, "Call no one blessed before his death." The Saviour is perfect in all things. No deceit shared his life, no deceit lived with him, no wickedness was ever present with him. "Tell that fox: today and tomorrow I perform signs, and on the third day I am perfected." If Christ called his own death perfection, who can imagine perfection before death?

And he departed until an opportune time, and then angels came and ministered to him. The goal of the discipline is to be served by angels. What the devil had brought up wrongly and at the wrong time, the Lover of humankind at once made plain. For the devil said, "He will command his angels concerning you." You brought it up at the wrong time; God did it at the right time and according to his plan, to show that a reward awaits those who contend: angels came and ministered to him. To whom? To the form of humanity, to the one who trampled on the demons, who trod on the asp and the basilisk, who set his foot on the lion and the dragon. For if he had not trodden on them first himself, he would not have given us authority to tread on the lion and the dragon.
The first contest is the one against the demons,

since Moses and Elijah stand forty days [?]. Moses fasted, but not to accomplish what Christ accomplished. Moses did not drive off [?] the demons by fasting. Nor did Elijah fast to overthrow the devil; rather, Jesus overcame [?] these things. He accomplishes the deeds, as he had foretold. The Master of the law and the prophets set Moses and Elijah beside him. The Master of the evangelists set Peter and John and James beside him. And a single cloud forms, as a type of the Church, and having indicated to that one in a worthy manner [?] what Moses would have said, a living voice [?]. This voice the Father confirmed on the mountain, saying, "This is my beloved Son; listen to him." For Moses had proclaimed beforehand: "The Lord our God will raise up for you a prophet like me; listen to him." This was to show that grace did not do violence to the law but fulfilled the law, not insulting Moses but fulfilling his word. Not by necessity, but through the law and the prophets the royal tokens [?] of the truth are received.

For just as the images of a king are honoured before he arrives, but once the king appears, the whole display of the image falls idle and the title passes back to the original, so it is here. Before Christ there were the law and the prophets, but after Christ the things of the Godhead shine forth and the things of humanity fall idle [?]. In this humanity it came about that we are all saved, in Christ himself, to whom be glory, might and honour to the ages of ages. Amen.
